questions.q: What key assumption do Dynamic Programming methods make that distinguishes them from Monte Carlo and TD methods?
options: They assume the reward is always positive
They assume a perfect model of the environment — P(s'|s,a) and R(s,a,s') are known exactly
They assume the policy is always deterministic
They assume there is only one state in the environment
questions.explain: DP methods require a fully known model of the environment's transition and reward functions, unlike Monte Carlo and TD methods, which learn from sampled experience without needing this model.

options: The optimal policy π* directly, in one step
V^π(s) for every state, for a fixed policy π, via repeated application of the Bellman equation
The reward function R(s,a,s')
The transition probabilities P(s'|s,a)
questions.explain: Policy evaluation repeatedly sweeps through all states, applying the Bellman equation for V^π as an update rule, until the value estimates converge to the true V^π.

questions.q: What does the policy improvement theorem guarantee?
options: That a randomly chosen policy is always optimal
That acting greedily with respect to V^π produces a policy that is at least as good as π, and usually strictly better
That V^π always equals zero
That the discount factor must be 1
questions.explain: If the greedy policy with respect to V^π differs from π, it's guaranteed to perform at least as well, and typically better — this is the policy improvement theorem.

questions.q: How does value iteration differ from policy iteration?
options: Value iteration never converges to the optimal value function
Value iteration takes just one sweep of evaluation per iteration, using the Bellman optimality equation directly, rather than fully evaluating the policy each time
Value iteration does not require knowledge of P or R
Value iteration only works for continuing tasks
questions.explain: Value iteration folds evaluation and improvement into a single update per sweep by applying max_a directly, rather than running full policy evaluation to convergence before each improvement step.

questions.q: Why doesn't Dynamic Programming scale well to most real-world RL problems?
options: It only works with stochastic policies
It requires a fully known model and must sweep over every state, which becomes intractable as the state space grows (the curse of dimensionality)
DP cannot use a discount factor
DP only applies to episodic tasks
questions.explain: DP needs an exact model of the environment and performs full sweeps over the entire state space, which is both unavailable and computationally intractable for most large or unknown real-world environments.
